newsitem.title: UK: IBCA gives Lithuania BB plus long-term rating.
newsitem.headline: IBCA gives Lithuania BB plus long-term rating.

text.p: IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said on Tuesday it had assigned a BB plus long-term foreign currency rating to the Republic of Lithuania, its first formal rating of the country.

"The rating will apply to senior, unsecured sovereign debt issues and serve as a ceiling for IBCA credit ratings of banks and corporates in Lithuania," IBCA said. The statement confirmed a statement from the Lithuanian government on Friday.
IBCA also assigned a short-term foreign currency rating of B, and a rating of BBB plus for local currency-denominated government debt.
It said this reflected the low level of Treasury debt both in absolute and in relative terms, and a positive outlook for inflation, which is on a steadily declining trend.

"The Lithuanian economy is recovering well from a particularly harsh recession in its transition to a market-oriented economy, suffered largely because of an unusually high dependence on cheap Russian energy imports," the agency said.

"Macro-economic stabilisation has been delivered via tough controls on public spending and a currency board system which pegs the currency at 4.0 litas:$1.0. So far, the fixed rate does not appear to have undermined export performance, which has been sustained by large initial reserves of competitiveness and considerable flexibility in real wages," IBCA said.
"Nonetheless, the present administration's plans gradually to change the exchange rate system may be timely."

IBCA said although recent revised official figures suggested a current account deficit more than three times larger than previously estimated, the deficit was now declining and was probably overstated due to the under-recording of exports.
"The new Government's plans for fiscal tightening are a further assurance that any problem that emerges will be tackled," IBCA said.
It said broad consensus on the policies needed to reform the economy and assure macro-economic stability was underpinned by a desire to participate in the European Union and the Atlantic Alliance.

"In the process of strengthening ties with western Europe, Lithuania can also build a comparative advantage based on its geographic position at the cross-roads between Russia and the Baltic Sea, and between Poland and the St Petersburg region," IBCA said.

"Lithuania benefits from very low levels of debt, in relation both to GDP and to foreign exchange receipts, and for the time being, very low debt service ratios. This has been a function of gaining independence in 1991 with no debt because of the Russian Federation's assumption of the debts (and assets) of the former Soviet Union."
But IBCA said the rating was constrained by the lack of a track record for new national institutions, from the banking sector through the statistical office to main offices of state.
Moreover, IBCA said Lithuania's foreign exchange reserves, although rising, were presently below the traditional comfort threshold of three months of import cover.
